title: The impact of a virtual teaching assistant (chatbot) on students’ learning in Ghanaian higher education
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a virtual teaching assistant chatbot can improve student learning in a higher-education context characterized by limited student–instructor interaction and high student–teacher ratios. The core research question is how the KNUSTbot, used as an intermediary between students and instructors, affects learning in an undergraduate multimedia programming course. The study also investigates students’ perceptions of learning with the chatbot.

The intervention was a zero-coding AI chatbot called KNUSTbot, built with Flow XO and integrated into WhatsApp. It was trained on prior course-related query data and additional online resources to answer students’ questions about HTML and CSS. All students received face-to-face instruction in the course, but the experimental group used a WhatsApp channel integrated with the chatbot for content-related questions, while the control group used a WhatsApp channel where they interacted with the course instructor instead. The study used a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest comparison plus post-intervention focus groups with the experimental group.

Participants were 68 final-year undergraduate students in a multimedia programming course in the Department of Publishing Studies at Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology in Ghana. The intervention lasted 16 weeks during the second semester of the 2021 academic year. Quantitative outcomes were measured with an achievement test, and qualitative data came from focus groups about the chatbot experience.

The main conclusion is that students in the chatbot condition outperformed students in the instructor-interaction control condition on posttest academic achievement. Focus group findings suggested that students valued the chatbot’s ease of use, immediate feedback, and access to supplementary resources, and many reported increased confidence. However, students also identified drawbacks: some responses were outdated or irrelevant, explanations were not always deep enough, and the chatbot lacked detailed follow-up interaction and support for applying knowledge. The authors conclude that chatbots can be a useful, low-cost support tool in resource-constrained higher-education settings, but they should not be assumed to replace the depth and adaptability of human instruction.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study with a comparison group, reported statistical testing, and mixed-method triangulation, but it is not a fully convincing RCT and is limited to one course at one university with a small sample. It meets a moderate evidence standard with some credibility concerns.
impact_tier_rationale: The academic outcome shows a large positive impact, with very large reported partial eta squared values (0.570-0.740) and sizable posttest mean differences favoring the chatbot group. However, impact is demonstrated in higher education programming, not the target K-12 writing-feedback context.

interventions.use_case: Zero-coding WhatsApp-based virtual teaching assistant chatbot answering undergraduate multimedia programming questions (HTML/CSS) outside class as an intermediary between students and instructor.

finding.finding_summary: In a pretest-posttest quasi-experiment with 68 final-year undergraduates (34 chatbot, 34 instructor-control), students using the KNUSTbot improved from M=40.6 (SD=4.95) to M=81.1 (SD=3.19), while controls improved from M=43.4 (SD=4.09) to M=65.2 (SD=3.73) on a multimedia programming achievement test. The time-by-cohort interaction was significant, F(1,66)=188, p<.001, with partial eta squared=0.740; the between-group posttest effect was also significant, F(1,66)=87.5, p<.001, partial eta squared=0.570.
finding.measure: Course achievement test in multimedia programming (objective items plus practical HTML/CSS exam)
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.740 (interaction); partial eta squared=0.570 (between-group posttest effect)
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI pretest experimental 38.9-42.2; pretest control 42.0-44.7; posttest experimental 80.1-82.2; posttest control 64.0-66.5
finding.std_deviation: Experimental pre SD=4.95, post SD=3.19; Control pre SD=4.09, post SD=3.73

finding.finding_summary: Focus-group data from the 34 students in the chatbot condition indicated generally positive perceptions, especially around immediate feedback, ease of use, and increased confidence/self-belief in learning. Theme frequencies included immediate feedback (15/34, 44.1%), ease of use (10/34, 29.4%), and more self-belief to learn effectively (4/34, 11.7%); 27/34 (79.4%) recommended using chatbots in more courses.
finding.measure: Post-intervention focus groups on satisfaction, confidence, engagement, and perceived learning support

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that chatbot use sometimes supported independent information seeking and verification, with some saying it helped them find answers on their own and evaluate linked resources. However, many also reported limitations for deeper thinking and application, including inability to get sufficiently detailed explanations (11/34, 32.4%) and a dearth of detailed interactions (20/34, 58.8%), suggesting uneven support for higher-order thinking and knowledge transfer.
finding.measure: Focus-group perceptions of information seeking, depth of thinking, and application of knowledge

finding.finding_summary: The study presents qualitative and usage evidence that the chatbot provided 24/7 rapid responses, especially during evening hours (20:00-22:00) when instructors were typically unavailable, suggesting improved responsiveness and reduced reliance on instructor time. Operational benefits are discussed rather than directly measured, with authors arguing the tool may reduce instructor workload in high student-instructor-ratio settings.
finding.measure: Engagement logs by time of day and qualitative reports of immediacy/workload relief
